paragraphs: MalNet is a database for studying how machine learning represents graphs. Its central design choice is to combine three properties: large individual graphs, a large number of graphs, and diverse classes. The authors argue that existing graph databases do not bring all three together, restricting how researchers can distinguish the strengths and weaknesses of different methods.

The graphs describe function calls in malicious software. MalNet contains more than 1.2 million graphs, with averages exceeding 15,000 nodes and 35,000 edges per graph. Its labels form a hierarchy of 47 types and 696 families. This gives researchers both substantial graph structure to process and many categories to distinguish.

The paper analyzes the database’s origins and properties and evaluates machine learning methods, including graph neural networks. Its contribution is a demanding shared resource for comparisons. The scale and category diversity also create opportunities to investigate uneven class representation, explainability, and differences in classification difficulty; these are research possibilities enabled by the dataset.
neurips-2021-a-large-scale-database-for-.tldr: MalNet combines over 1.2 million large software graphs with diverse hierarchical labels to broaden evaluation of graph learning methods.

paragraphs: This paper examines why reported machine learning advances sometimes weaken under closer examination or apply less broadly than expected. The authors review 107 survey papers spanning language processing, recommendation, vision, reinforcement learning, computational biology, graph learning, and other areas. They organize recurring criticisms into a taxonomy of evaluation failures.

The first category is internal validity: whether an evaluation supports its conclusions within the particular learning problem being studied. Examples include unfair comparisons with baseline methods and overfitting caused by repeated use of a test set. These problems affect how much confidence a reader should place in an apparent improvement on the evaluated task.

The second category is external validity: whether results on one learning problem carry over to other problems. Progress on a benchmark may not translate into progress on tasks that seem related. Separating these categories helps make evaluation criticism more precise, distinguishing weaknesses in a comparison itself from weaknesses in the broader conclusions drawn from that comparison.
neurips-2021-are-we-learning-yet-a-meta-.tldr: A review of 107 surveys organizes recurring machine learning evaluation failures around validity within tasks and generalization across tasks.

paragraphs: ARKitScenes supports research on understanding indoor spaces from mobile color and depth recordings. Its motivation is the growing availability of depth sensors in commonly used devices. That availability creates opportunities for practical applications, but the authors emphasize that bringing scene understanding methods into everyday experiences still requires further development.

The dataset includes raw and processed mobile recordings, high resolution depth maps from a stationary laser scanner, and manually annotated three-dimensional boxes around furniture. The boxes include object orientation. Together, these resources provide mobile observations, more detailed depth references, and object annotations for studying different aspects of indoor scene understanding.

The authors investigate two tasks: detecting objects in three dimensions and using color images to increase depth-map resolution. They report that the dataset can help advance existing methods while presenting challenges that better reflect real environments. The contribution connects data from accessible mobile sensors with richer reference measurements, supporting evaluation of methods intended to operate on those mobile observations.
neurips-2021-arkitscenes-a-diverse-real-.tldr: ARKitScenes pairs mobile indoor color and depth recordings with detailed reference data for 3D detection and depth enhancement.

paragraphs: BEIR evaluates whether text retrieval systems work beyond the narrow settings in which they are commonly studied. It combines 18 public datasets covering different tasks and domains. This diversity makes generalization a central part of evaluation, allowing researchers to examine retrieval effectiveness across a broader range of conditions.

The authors compare 10 systems representing lexical, sparse, dense, late-interaction, and re-ranking approaches. Their results identify BM25 as a robust baseline. Re-ranking and late-interaction methods achieve the strongest zero-shot results on average, but require substantial computation. The average qualification matters: the finding describes performance across the benchmark rather than establishing a winner for every individual task.

Dense and sparse retrieval approaches are more computationally efficient in these comparisons, yet often perform worse than other approaches. This exposes a trade-off between retrieval quality and computational cost, along with room to improve generalization. BEIR supplies a shared framework for examining that trade-off across varied retrieval settings.
neurips-2021-beir-a-heterogeneous-benchm.tldr: BEIR compares retrieval systems across 18 diverse datasets, revealing generalization gaps and trade-offs between zero-shot quality and computation.

paragraphs: Complex query answering asks models to reason over knowledge graphs using combinations of simpler operations. A key question is whether learning those operations allows a model to handle more elaborate formulas. This paper calls that ability combinatorial generalizability and introduces EFO-1-QA to evaluate it across a wider range of query structures.

The dataset contains 301 query types, around 20 times the variety in existing datasets described by the authors. It also supports comparisons across seven choices of operator systems and nine forms of complex queries. This design lets researchers study both the operations used to express a query and the form in which those operations are assembled.

The authors examine projection and intersection in detail and investigate how query forms affect models when the operator choice is fixed. The contribution makes the structure of reasoning itself an explicit evaluation dimension. The accompanying code and data provide a pipeline for comparing complex query answering models along these dimensions.
neurips-2021-benchmarking-the-combinator.tldr: EFO-1-QA tests how knowledge-graph query models generalize across 301 query types, different operators, and alternative query forms.

paragraphs: BiToD addresses the evaluation of conversational systems that help users complete tasks in more than one language. The authors identify a gap in existing end-to-end dialogue datasets, which focus on a single language. They introduce a bilingual dataset spanning multiple domains so that multilingual dialogue development can be studied within a shared benchmark.

The dataset contains more than 7,000 dialogues and 144,000 utterances, together with a large bilingual knowledge base designed to be realistic. Baselines cover three settings: learning within one language, learning bilingually, and transferring learning across languages. These settings make it possible to examine how language sharing affects dialogue systems under different training conditions.

The baseline analysis supports the effectiveness of training a bilingual system compared with training two separate monolingual systems. It also points to the potential of a bilingual knowledge base and cross-language transfer when resources are limited. These findings motivate shared bilingual training while leaving the strength of the low-resource claim as a demonstrated possibility.
neurips-2021-bitod-a-bilingual-multi-dom.tldr: BiToD benchmarks bilingual task-oriented dialogue and finds benefits from shared training, with potential gains from cross-language transfer under limited resources.

paragraphs: CrowdSpeech addresses a difficulty in collecting speech data through crowdsourcing: combining contributors’ transcriptions into reliable results. Crowdsourcing is established for simpler tasks such as image classification, but the authors argue that speech lacks sufficiently developed aggregation methods. Developing those methods is itself hindered by a shortage of suitable training data.

The paper introduces a large public dataset of crowdsourced audio transcriptions and evaluates both existing and new aggregation approaches on it. Those evaluations show room for improvement. The dataset therefore serves as material for learning aggregation methods and as a common basis for comparing how well different methods combine crowd contributions.

The authors also design a repeatable collection pipeline for new domains and demonstrate it by creating VoxDIY for Russian, described here as an under-resourced language. They release code for reproducing the full pipeline and share collection practices. This extends the contribution beyond one dataset to a methodology for constructing further speech transcription resources through crowdsourcing.
neurips-2021-crowdspeech-and-vox-diy-ben.tldr: CrowdSpeech and VoxDIY provide crowdsourced transcription data and a reproducible collection pipeline to support better aggregation methods.

paragraphs: CUAD targets a practical obstacle to applying language models in specialized fields: producing labeled examples requires costly expert work. The authors address this in legal contract review by working with dozens of legal experts from The Atticus Project. The resulting dataset contains more than 13,000 annotations for training and evaluating language processing systems.

The task is to highlight contract passages that deserve a human reviewer’s attention. This gives models a concrete role in the review process: identifying relevant portions of the text for further examination. Expert annotations provide examples of what counts as salient material in this specialized setting, making the task available for systematic machine learning research.

Experiments show early capabilities in Transformer models, with performance strongly affected by model design and training dataset size. The authors describe these results as promising while emphasizing substantial remaining room for improvement. CUAD therefore contributes both a specialized expert-labeled resource and a challenging benchmark for studying how language models handle contract review.
neurips-2021-cuad-an-expert-annotated-nl.tldr: CUAD supplies expert annotations for highlighting important contract passages, exposing promising but still limited Transformer performance.

paragraphs: DEBAGREEMENT is a dataset for identifying whether a reply agrees with, disagrees with, or is neutral toward an earlier comment. It contains 42,894 labeled comment-reply pairs from five Reddit forums discussing political and social topics. The task concerns the relationship between two contributions to a discussion, making the reply’s context central to what is being classified.

The authors select comment pairs so that they collectively form a user interaction graph within each forum. The dataset also contains language features common in online exchanges, including slang, sarcasm, and topic-specific jokes. These features make agreement detection challenging because the relationship between comments can be expressed indirectly.

The paper evaluates language models and investigates graph structure, authorship, and timing as contextual information. Its design creates opportunities to combine text-based methods with methods that use relationships among users and comments. The abstract motivates these combinations through prior findings about context, while presenting the dataset as a resource for investigating their usefulness in online agreement detection.
neurips-2021-debagreement-a-comment-repl.tldr: DEBAGREEMENT pairs labeled Reddit exchanges with interaction context to study agreement detection in challenging online language.

paragraphs: DENETHOR supports research on identifying crop types from satellite observations collected over time. Crops change during their growing cycles, and these differences can help distinguish them. The authors focus on a growing opportunity: satellite imagery is becoming available nearly every day, but deep learning has made limited use of that dense sequence of observations.

The dataset covers Northern Germany and combines daily, analysis-ready Planet Fusion data with Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 optical time series. This gives researchers observations with both spatial detail and repeated measurements through time. The central modeling question is how to use that combined information effectively for crop classification.

Baseline experiments suggest that fully exploiting the available spatial and temporal information may require specially designed architectures. The dataset poses two connected challenges: improving classification through the temporal dimension and handling a shift to a different year. Success therefore involves learning from crop development over time while remaining effective when the year of observation changes.
neurips-2021-denethor-the-dynamicearthne.tldr: DENETHOR combines daily satellite observations for crop classification, challenging models to exploit time and generalize across years.

paragraphs: FEVEROUS expands fact verification to include information stored in tables alongside ordinary text. The authors argue that earlier large benchmarks largely emphasize textual sources, overlooking structured information. Their dataset contains 87,026 verified claims, creating a shared setting for systems that must work with both kinds of evidence.

Each claim is linked to Wikipedia sentences, table cells, or a combination of the two. A label states whether the evidence supports the claim, refutes it, or leaves insufficient information for a verdict. This connects the final decision to identified supporting material and requires the task to accommodate different evidence formats.

The authors describe efforts to track and reduce exploitable dataset biases, including shortcuts that allow label prediction without consulting evidence. They also build a baseline that gets both the evidence and verdict correct for 18% of claims. That joint result indicates substantial difficulty in completing the full verification task, where finding the right material and reaching the right conclusion must both succeed.
neurips-2021-feverous-fact-extraction-an.tldr: FEVEROUS benchmarks claim verification using Wikipedia text and tables, with a baseline solving evidence retrieval and verdict prediction jointly for 18% of claims.

paragraphs: The Graph Robustness Benchmark addresses inconsistent comparisons between attacks on graph learning models and the defenses designed to resist them. The authors identify a problem with the surrounding arms race: competing methods are often evaluated under different or unrealistic conditions. GRB aims to make those comparisons more unified, reproducible, and scalable.

The benchmark combines diverse datasets, modular attack and defense implementations, and a common evaluation protocol across defined scenarios. Its modular organization lets researchers develop components within a shared pipeline. Automated data processing and experimental evaluation reduce the amount of surrounding infrastructure needed to study a new robust graph model.

The authors provide baseline experiments with existing techniques and public leaderboards for different scenarios. These establish starting points for comparison and support open research. The main contribution is an evaluation framework that makes experimental conditions more consistent, giving subsequent attack and defense results a clearer basis for comparison within the scenarios the benchmark defines.
neurips-2021-graph-robustness-benchmark-.tldr: GRB standardizes datasets, attack and defense implementations, and evaluation scenarios for reproducible comparisons of graph model robustness.

paragraphs: HumBugDB provides acoustic recordings for detecting mosquitoes and identifying their species from wingbeat sounds. The motivation is to support mosquito surveys that could inform outbreak prediction and intervention policy. The dataset contains 20 hours of expertly labeled, precisely timed audio, with 18 hours carrying annotations covering 36 species.

Recordings span mosquitoes raised in cages and mosquitoes captured in the wild. They include indoor and outdoor backgrounds from five countries and vary in how clearly mosquito sounds stand out from noise. This variation addresses the challenge of obtaining recordings from realistic conditions. A database also preserves metadata such as capture method, age, feeding status, and sex.

The authors document collection and curation and provide code for feature extraction and Bayesian convolutional neural network training. Two tasks are supported: detecting mosquitoes against their acoustic backgrounds and classifying detected mosquitoes by species. The resource connects machine learning research on difficult audio signals with domain research on mosquito behavior, distribution, and associated threats.
neurips-2021-humbugdb-a-large-scale-acou.tldr: HumBugDB supplies annotated mosquito audio across species and environments for acoustic detection and species classification.

paragraphs: LiRo creates a common platform for evaluating Romanian language models. Its motivation is an uneven distribution of research infrastructure: large datasets and standardized benchmarks have supported progress in language processing, but many languages lack comparable resources. The platform provides task-specific leaderboards with baseline results to establish shared reference points.

It covers nine standard tasks, including text classification, translation, sentiment analysis, question answering, and sentence similarity. It also includes tasks involving entities, grammatical structure, and language modeling. A further task concerns reducing gender bias in embeddings, bringing a social concern into the evaluation alongside conventional language capabilities.

The authors add three datasets: one built from Romanian Wikipedia and two created by translating existing sentence-similarity and question-answering datasets into Romanian. These additions expand the material available for Romanian evaluation. The authors also suggest that the translated resources could support multilingual research by augmenting parallel corpora, giving the platform potential relevance beyond models evaluated solely in Romanian.
neurips-2021-liro-benchmark-and-leaderbo.tldr: LiRo brings task-specific benchmarks, baselines, and new datasets to Romanian NLP, including an evaluation task for gender debiasing.

paragraphs: ONCE supports research on three-dimensional object detection for autonomous driving, particularly methods that learn from large amounts of unlabeled data. The authors motivate it through the heavy dependence of perception systems on annotations, including annotations needed to cover unusual cases. They identify insufficient real-world scene data as an obstacle to exploring alternative learning approaches.

The dataset contains one million LiDAR scenes and seven million corresponding camera images, selected from 144 driving hours. Collection spans different areas, times, and weather conditions. This combination provides substantial scene data and varied recording conditions for studying three-dimensional perception in a driving setting.

The paper also supplies a benchmark that reproduces and evaluates multiple self-supervised and semi-supervised methods. Its analyses examine performance in relation to the amount of data used. The contribution therefore combines a large data resource with a framework for investigating data scale, supporting research into how unlabeled observations can contribute to object detection alongside labeled examples.
neurips-2021-one-million-scenes-for-auto.tldr: ONCE provides one million LiDAR scenes and a benchmark for studying how unlabeled data scale affects 3D driving perception.

paragraphs: The Ludwig Benchmarking Toolkit addresses model comparisons shaped by a user’s own priorities. A benchmark centered on average accuracy may be insufficient when other objectives matter, and differences in training resources can complicate comparisons. LBT provides a configurable way to run benchmark studies with explicit training controls and multiple evaluation objectives.

The toolkit covers the process from hyperparameter optimization through evaluation. Users can extend its tasks, models, datasets, and metrics while using a standardized training framework intended to control confounding variables. This makes the conditions of comparison part of the study’s design, alongside the choice of what outcomes to measure.

The authors demonstrate the toolkit through text classification experiments covering seven models and nine datasets. They examine prediction speed versus performance, relationships between dataset properties and results, and how pretraining affects convergence and robustness. These studies illustrate how the same toolkit can answer different practical benchmarking questions, depending on the objectives and constraints a user chooses.
neurips-2021-personalized-benchmarking-w.tldr: LBT enables customizable, controlled model comparisons that account for multiple objectives such as prediction performance and inference latency.

paragraphs: Pl@ntNet-300K is designed to evaluate classifiers that can return a set of candidate labels. Plant identification provides a demanding setting because different species can look very similar. The dataset comes from the Pl@ntNet citizen observatory and contains 306,146 images representing 1,081 species.

Two properties shape the challenge. First, a small number of species account for most images, leaving an uneven distribution of examples across classes. Second, visual resemblance between species can make identification difficult even for experts. These characteristics make the dataset useful for investigating predictions that retain several possible species when the image is ambiguous.

The authors recommend mean top-k accuracy and mean average-k accuracy as evaluation measures for this setting. They also provide a baseline using a deep neural network trained with cross-entropy loss. Together, the data, proposed metrics, and baseline establish a comparison point for set-valued classification methods under both strong class imbalance and substantial visual ambiguity.
neurips-2021-pl-ntnet-300k-a-plant-image.tldr: Pl@ntNet-300K tests set-valued plant classification using visually ambiguous species and a strongly imbalanced image distribution.

paragraphs: Q-Pain is a dataset for assessing social bias in medical question answering about pain management. The authors motivate it with the contrast between language systems’ fluent responses and their tendency to reflect social biases. Pain treatment is the specific decision-making setting in which the dataset makes those concerns available for systematic study.

The contribution includes an evaluation framework and a sample experimental design for measuring potential bias in treatment decisions. This gives researchers both material to evaluate and a proposed structure for conducting the evaluation. The focus is on whether treatment responses differ across social groups, connecting model behavior to a consequential medical use case.

The authors demonstrate the framework with GPT-2 and GPT-3 and find statistically significant treatment differences across subgroups defined jointly by race and gender. These results provide evidence of disparities in the evaluated systems and setting. They support the authors’ call for targeted bias assessment before medical deployment, with Q-Pain offered as a resource for that assessment.
neurips-2021-q-pain-a-question-answering.tldr: Q-Pain evaluates bias in pain-management question answering and finds significant treatment differences across race-gender subgroups in GPT-2 and GPT-3.

paragraphs: RELLISUR addresses images that are difficult to see because they are both dark and low resolution. The authors observe that low-light enhancement and super-resolution have generally been studied separately, even though real images can suffer from both problems at once. They introduce paired data to support studying the combined restoration task.

The dataset contains 12,750 image pairs spanning different resolutions and low-light levels. Each degraded image is paired with a normally lit, high resolution reference. These pairs support training models to map directly from poor visibility to an image with greater sharpness and detail, bringing both enhancement goals into a single learning problem.

The paper benchmarks existing methods for the separate tasks and experiments with joint enhancement. In the reported experiments, joint processing yields more accurate reconstructions and better perceptual quality than processing the tasks sequentially. This finding supports investigating combined methods and establishes RELLISUR as a resource for comparing approaches to simultaneous lighting and resolution improvement.
neurips-2021-rellisur-a-real-low-light-i.tldr: RELLISUR provides paired data for simultaneous low-light enhancement and super-resolution, with experiments favoring joint over sequential processing.

paragraphs: SODA10M supports learning visual perception for autonomous driving from abundant unlabeled images and a smaller labeled collection. Its motivation is the difficulty of thoroughly annotating every driving situation, including different cities, lighting, and weather. The dataset provides a common setting for evaluating self-supervised and semi-supervised approaches at substantial scale.

It contains 10 million unlabeled images and 20,000 images annotated with six object categories. The images come from 27,833 driving hours across 32 cities, with variation in weather, time, and location. This breadth is intended to support exploration of large pretrained models using diverse driving observations.

The authors evaluate existing learning approaches and analyze their behavior in the driving domain. Their experiments indicate that SODA10M is a promising pretraining resource: self-supervised methods achieve superior downstream performance after fine-tuning for tasks including detection and semantic or instance segmentation. The result supports the usefulness of the dataset for representation learning across several driving perception tasks.
neurips-2021-soda10m-a-large-scale-2d-se.tldr: SODA10M combines 10 million unlabeled driving images with a smaller labeled set to benchmark learning methods that reduce annotation dependence.

paragraphs: STAR evaluates reasoning grounded in situations shown in real-world videos. Its videos contain human actions and interactions, and its questions concern interactions, event sequences, predictions, and feasibility. The benchmark asks models to connect what they observe with structured reasoning about the situation, including how events relate and what could happen.

The authors represent situations with hypergraphs linking entities and relations such as people, objects, and actions. Questions and answers are generated procedurally, and each question has a functional program describing the reasoning needed to answer it from the situation representation. This makes the intended answering logic explicit within the benchmark.

Existing video reasoning models evaluated by the authors all struggle with the task. To investigate the difficulty, the paper introduces a diagnostic neuro-symbolic model that separates visual perception, situation abstraction, language understanding, and functional reasoning. This decomposition supports examining distinct parts of the task, helping clarify where the demands of situated video reasoning arise.
neurips-2021-star-a-benchmark-for-situat.tldr: STAR combines real-world videos, structured situation representations, and explicit question logic to benchmark and diagnose situated reasoning.

paragraphs: This review examines datasets containing human-written or human-annotated explanations for language processing tasks. The authors identify 65 datasets and organize the literature around how explanations are collected. The focus is the data used to teach or assess explanation-producing models, making annotation practices the central object of study.

The review distinguishes three uses for these explanations. They can provide extra information to improve a predictive task, supervise models learning to explain their predictions, or serve as reference answers when evaluating generated explanations. These roles place explanation data at different points in model development, from training the predictor to judging the explanations it produces.

The authors group explanations into highlights, free text, and structured forms, then examine the strengths and shortcomings of their collection methods. They use this analysis to recommend practices for future datasets. The contribution is an organized account of explanation resources and annotation methodologies, helping researchers connect the kind of explanation they collect with how that data will be used.
neurips-2021-teach-me-to-explain-a-revie.tldr: This review organizes 65 explanation datasets by format and use, assesses annotation methods, and recommends future collection practices.

paragraphs: The Met Dataset studies recognition of individual artworks, with each museum exhibit treated as its own class. Built from the museum’s open collection, the training set covers about 224,000 classes using studio photographs. The challenge combines a large number of classes, uneven representation, and strong visual similarity between different exhibits.

Most testing uses photographs taken by museum visitors, introducing a shift from the controlled appearance of training images. Additional test images do not depict Met exhibits, adding a setting resembling out-of-distribution detection. Together, these tests examine recognition across photographic conditions and behavior when images fall outside the collection being recognized.

The authors evaluate several approaches to establish a comparison resource. They report that combining self-supervised and supervised contrastive learning effectively trains a visual backbone for non-parametric classification, identifying this as a promising direction. The benchmark also follows conventions from instance recognition in other domains to encourage methods whose usefulness can extend across different kinds of objects.
neurips-2021-the-met-dataset-instance-le.tldr: The Met Dataset benchmarks recognition of individual artworks across studio and visitor photographs, with additional tests on images outside the collection.

paragraphs: ThreeDWorld is a simulation platform for studying agents that perceive and interact with three-dimensional environments. It combines visual and audio rendering with physical interactions between agents and objects. Its purpose is to support experiments where sensory observations and changes in the physical world are available within the same interactive system.

The platform offers near-photorealistic images in real time, detailed audio, customizable objects and environments, and procedures for generating new environments. Its physics includes materials such as cloth, liquids, and deformable objects. Customizable avatars embody agents, while virtual reality support allows human interaction. The API supports multiple agents and returns both sensor observations and information about the simulated physical state.

The authors present initial experiments spanning machine learning, computer vision, and cognitive science. Examples include physical scene understanding through multiple senses, dynamics prediction, interactions among agents, child-like learning models, and attention studies. These demonstrations illustrate the platform’s range as experimental infrastructure for investigating perception, action, and physical understanding together.
neurips-2021-threedworld-a-platform-for-.tldr: ThreeDWorld combines interactive physics, visual and audio simulation, and agent control for research on perception and behavior.

paragraphs: An autonomous vehicle’s high-definition map can become outdated when the physical world changes. This paper studies how to detect those changes by checking whether sensor observations still agree with the map. The task makes agreement between stored map information and observed surroundings something a learned system can assess.

The authors introduce Trust, but Verify, which they describe as the first dataset for this task. They assembled it by mining thousands of hours from more than nine months of autonomous vehicle fleet operations. It includes maps and driving logs from six North American cities and more than 7.9 million images, providing a substantial collection for studying map agreement.

The paper presents learning-based approaches using both a bird’s-eye view and the vehicle’s own perspective. Its training strategy addresses the rarity of actual map changes: because vector maps are straightforward to alter synthetically, the authors rely on simulated data to train their model. This makes synthetic map manipulation central to learning from a phenomenon that occurs infrequently in real driving.

The stated finding is that models trained this way can generalize to real-world data distributions. That supports the usefulness of simulated training examples for this task without establishing that transfer will succeed in every setting. The authors also publicly release the dataset, code, and models under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license.
neurips-2021-trust-but-verify-cross-moda.tldr: Trust, but Verify introduces a dataset and learning-based approaches for detecting HD map changes, showing that models trained with simulated data can generalize to real-world data.
